And I'm here with Elio from Imprinted Circuits.
You're probably one of the few remaining Australian suppliers and manufacturers of bare printed circuit boards.
We're down to the very last few.
There's one smaller one in Victoria that's still manufacturing, and we do have another competitor in the ACT.
But as far as our type of processing goes, we're probably one of the largest left in Australia for manufacturing.
And we still have just under 50% of our business is still locally manufactured.
Okay, so what happened to the Australian printed circuit board PCB manufacturer?
Well, it didn't start with China.
It was a lot of the Asian countries started producing printed circuit boards.
And one of the things about printed circuit boards is 50% of the cost is labor.
So even though our material prices aren't much different, if you can reduce your labor cost significantly,
as the Asian competitors did, then you can have a significantly cheaper product.
As such, very difficult to compete.
You find people are coming back to Australia, though.
Because there's a few companies leaving China now because they're not that cheap anymore in terms of labor.
That's true, but the thing is, even though their labor prices are creeping up,
it's still not reaching the same sort of levels as we are in Australia.
So they're still competitive, still a better price than we are.
On top of it, the technologies in China have developed quite a bit over time.
They can do very good, high-quality, very high-layer count printed circuit boards.
So if we have customers that need something higher-layer count than eight layers…
Then we need to go to one of our Asian sources.
So it's not worthwhile investing in the technology, the machines to do the higher-layer count?
Well, the thing is the call for higher-layer count is very limited,
so the investment really wouldn't pay off locally here.
So that's really what it boils down to, is what are we going to get as a return for the higher investment.
But we're pretty pleased with the fact that we can still say we're very busy with our manufacturing,
and we have the support of our parent company, which helps a great deal as well.
So at the end of the day, we feel that the manufacturing side of it will be an ongoing viable part of our business moving forward.
So in terms of flexible PCBs, if people want those, they've still got to go overseas to get these flexible PCBs?
The flexible printed circuits are still something that, for us, it's an investment that would we get a return on,
and would we be able to be competitive with imported pricing?
At this point in time, we wouldn't be.
So that's something that we'll continue to import from China.

How long does it take to manufacture an eight-layer board?

But we can do a double-sided board in 24 hours.
So if a customer needed something urgently, we could certainly turn around a double-sided board in 24 hours and a four-layer in 48 hours.

Do you manufacture your own in-house tooling?
Do you actually print your own?

So that's all part of the process.

So we allow ourselves that time to make sure that we've got everything ready to go before we start manufacturing.
Because as you can imagine, once you've made an eight-layer board and you discover that something's gone wrong, it's just scrap.

As far as track and space?

And hole sizes, can you do micro?
